newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil soybean exports could reach 8.5 mln tonnes.
newsitem.headline: Brazil soybean exports could reach 8.5 mln tonnes.

text.p: Brazil's Vegetable Oil Industries Association (Abiove) now estimates Brazilian soybean exports in 1997/98 (February/January) could reach 8.5 million tonnes, up from a forecast of eight million in April.
Abiove's latest forecast compares with exports of 3.65 million tonnes in 1996/97 and 3.52 million tonnes in 1995/96.

Its revised estimate coincided with the latest export registration statistics to May 15 which showed registrations of 7.18 million tonnes by the middle of month against 2.98 million to the same period in 1996 and 2.61 million in 1995.

"Sales registrations for soybean exports showed a growth of 141 percent and 175 percent in relation to the two previous years, exceeding the amounts shipped throughout all of 1996 and of 1995," Abiove said.
Even with the high level of export registrations, independent consultants Safras e Mercado said it still believed exports in 1997/98 would only reach eight million tonnes.
"I think 8.5 million tonnes is too high as I think export registrations are coming to an end," said analyst Flavio Franco.
As a result of the higher export expectations, Abiove reduced its crushing forecast by 500,000 tonnes to 18 million.
Soymeal exports are now seen down at 8.9 million against a previous estimate of 9.3 million and 10.9 million in 1996/97.
Soyoil sales overseas are now expected to reach 850,000 tonnes against a figure of 950,000 tonnes in April and 1,35 million tonnes in 1996/97.

The high soybean sales, triggered by the lifting of the ICMS export tax last year which previously favored soyproducts, has hit processors at a time when other countries are slow to remove protectionist policies, Abiove said.

The elimination of the differential partly compensated the Brazilian industry for high import tariffs applied in various countries, Abiove council member Sergio Barroso said in a copy of a speech presented at last week's International Association of Seed Crushers in Budapest.
But at the same time it has left Brazilian processors in a weaker position compared with international competition.
"Brazil's competitive advantages are being annulled by the artificial protectionist practices of some countries that distort worldwide commerce," Barroso said.

"The Uruguay Round's commitments are very timid. The protection in various countries is very high and the tariff reduction rate is very slow. We definitely feel there is no real interest in having a level playing field," he added.

Considering current reductions of around 0.6 percent a year, the U.S. will take 23 years to bring the import tax on soyoil to the seven percent levied on main edible oils from the current 20.8 percent, Barroso said.
In the case of Japan, while the country's industries only use imported raw materials, soyoil imports are blocked by a tariff of around 30 percent, he added.
